claim: Gene duplication is long recognized as a potential source of genetic innovation.
source: Gene duplication is long recognized as a potential source of genetic innovation (Ohno, 1970).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ohno, 1970

claim: Gene conversion is the nonreciprocal transfer of sequence between homologous genetic regions.
source: Gene conversion, the nonreciprocal transfer of sequence between homologous genetic regions, is one outcome of recombination evident in diverse eukaryotes (Brown et al., 1972; Semple and Wolfe, 1999; Drouin, 2002; Rozen et al., 2003; Ezawa et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2007), as well as in bacterial and archaeal genomes (Santoyo and Romero, 2005; Soppa, 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies in eukaryotes, bacteria, and archaea

claim: Gene conversion is evident in diverse eukaryotes.
source: Gene conversion, the nonreciprocal transfer of sequence between homologous genetic regions, is one outcome of recombination evident in diverse eukaryotes (Brown et al., 1972; Semple and Wolfe, 1999; Drouin, 2002; Rozen et al., 2003; Ezawa et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2007), as well as in bacterial and archaeal genomes (Santoyo and Romero, 2005; Soppa, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Gene conversion is evident in bacterial and archaeal genomes.
source: Gene conversion, the nonreciprocal transfer of sequence between homologous genetic regions, is one outcome of recombination evident in diverse eukaryotes (Brown et al., 1972; Semple and Wolfe, 1999; Drouin, 2002; Rozen et al., 2003; Ezawa et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2007), as well as in bacterial and archaeal genomes (Santoyo and Romero, 2005; Soppa, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Santoyo and Romero, 2005; Soppa, 2011

claim: Gene conversion can result in a high degree of identity among duplicated gene copies, as in ribosomal RNA gene arrays.
source: Gene conversion can result in a high degree of identity among duplicated gene copies, as in ribosomal RNA gene arrays (Liao, 1999; Eickbush and Eickbush, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on ribosomal RNA gene arrays

claim: Gene conversion can generate sequence diversity in the human leukocyte antigen gene family.
source: However, in other cases, such as the human leukocyte antigen gene family (Zangenberg et al., 1995) or the transmembrane protein gene cassettes of some pathogenic bacteria (Santoyo and Romero, 2005), gene conversion can also generate sequence diversity.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zangenberg et al., 1995

claim: Gene conversion can generate sequence diversity in transmembrane protein gene cassettes of some pathogenic bacteria.
source: However, in other cases, such as the human leukocyte antigen gene family (Zangenberg et al., 1995) or the transmembrane protein gene cassettes of some pathogenic bacteria (Santoyo and Romero, 2005), gene conversion can also generate sequence diversity.
evidence: Supported by citation to Santoyo and Romero, 2005

claim: Multiple gene copies create more targets for mutation.
source: Because multiple gene copies create more targets for mutation, variants that arise within individual copies can be efficiently spread or eliminated through gene conversion (Mano and Innan, 2008; Ellison and Bachtrog, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations and logical reasoning

claim: Variants that arise within individual gene copies can be efficiently spread or eliminated through gene conversion.
source: Because multiple gene copies create more targets for mutation, variants that arise within individual copies can be efficiently spread or eliminated through gene conversion (Mano and Innan, 2008; Ellison and Bachtrog, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mano and Innan, 2008; Ellison and Bachtrog, 2015

claim: Many studies to date have used phylogenetic analyses in relatively slow-evolving populations to infer outcomes of gene conversion.
source: Although recombination might influence genetic variation in populations on very short time scales, many studies to date have used phylogenetic analyses in relatively slow-evolving populations to infer outcomes of gene conversion, including cases of concerted evolution, where similarity between genes of a gene family within a species exceeds the similarity of orthologous genes between species (Chen et al., 2007; Ohta, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2007; Ohta, 2010

claim: Concerted evolution is where similarity between genes of a gene family within a species exceeds the similarity of orthologous genes between species.
source: Although recombination might influence genetic variation in populations on very short time scales, many studies to date have used phylogenetic analyses in relatively slow-evolving populations to infer outcomes of gene conversion, including cases of concerted evolution, where similarity between genes of a gene family within a species exceeds the similarity of orthologous genes between species (Chen et al., 2007; Ohta, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations and definition provided

claim: Extensive studies in yeast and bacteria have considered gene conversion on shorter time scales.
source: Extensive studies in yeast and bacteria (reviewed in Petes and Hill, 1988; Perkins, 1992; Haber, 2000; Santoyo and Romero, 2005), and some recent work in viruses (Hughes, 2004; Ba Abdullah et al., 2017), consider gene conversion on shorter time scales.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple review articles

claim: Some recent work in viruses has considered gene conversion on shorter time scales.
source: Extensive studies in yeast and bacteria (reviewed in Petes and Hill, 1988; Perkins, 1992; Haber, 2000; Santoyo and Romero, 2005), and some recent work in viruses (Hughes, 2004; Ba Abdullah et al., 2017), consider gene conversion on shorter time scales.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hughes, 2004; Ba Abdullah et al., 2017

claim: Poxviruses possess high rates of recombination.
source: Poxviruses are an intriguing system to study mechanisms of rapid adaptation, as they possess high rates of recombination (Ball, 1987; Evans et al., 1988; Spyropoulos et al., 1988; Merchlinsky, 1989) that lead to the recurrent emergence of tandem gene duplications (Slabaugh et al., 1989; Elde et al., 2012; Brennan et al., 2014; Erlandson et al., 2014; Cone et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: High rates of recombination in poxviruses lead to the recurrent emergence of tandem gene duplications.
source: Poxviruses are an intriguing system to study mechanisms of rapid adaptation, as they possess high rates of recombination (Ball, 1987; Evans et al., 1988; Spyropoulos et al., 1988; Merchlinsky, 1989) that lead to the recurrent emergence of tandem gene duplications (Slabaugh et al., 1989; Elde et al., 2012; Brennan et al., 2014; Erlandson et al., 2014; Cone et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The poxvirus DNA polymerase gene encodes both replicase and recombinase activities.
source: The poxvirus DNA polymerase gene encodes both replicase and recombinase activities, reflecting a tight coupling of these essential functions for virus replication (Colinas et al., 1990; Willer et al., 1999; Hamilton and Evans, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Colinas et al., 1990; Willer et al., 1999; Hamilton and Evans, 2005

claim: Polymerase-associated recombination may underlie the rapid appearance of gene copy number variation.
source: Polymerase-associated recombination may underlie the rapid appearance of gene copy number variation (CNV), which was proposed as a potentially widespread mechanism of vaccinia virus adaptation in response to strong selective pressure (Elde et al., 2012; Cone et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations and speculation

claim: Recurrent duplications of the K3L gene were identified following serial infections of human cells with a vaccinia strain lacking a strong PKR inhibitor encoded by the E3L gene.
source: In these studies, recurrent duplications of the K3L gene, which encodes a weak inhibitor of the human innate immune factor Protein Kinase R (PKR; Davies et al., 1992), were identified following serial infections of human cells with a vaccinia strain lacking a strong PKR inhibitor encoded by the E3L gene (ΔE3L; Chang et al., 1992; Beattie et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: K3L encodes a weak inhibitor of the human innate immune factor Protein Kinase R (PKR).
source: In these studies, recurrent duplications of the K3L gene, which encodes a weak inhibitor of the human innate immune factor Protein Kinase R (PKR; Davies et al., 1992), were identified following serial infections of human cells with a vaccinia strain lacking a strong PKR inhibitor encoded by the E3L gene (ΔE3L; Chang et al., 1992; Beattie et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Davies et al., 1992

claim: E3L encodes a strong PKR inhibitor.
source: In these studies, recurrent duplications of the K3L gene, which encodes a weak inhibitor of the human innate immune factor Protein Kinase R (PKR; Davies et al., 1992), were identified following serial infections of human cells with a vaccinia strain lacking a strong PKR inhibitor encoded by the E3L gene (ΔE3L; Chang et al., 1992; Beattie et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chang et al., 1992; Beattie et al., 1995

claim: A beneficial single nucleotide variant arose in the K3L gene in some populations, resulting in a His47Arg amino acid change.
source: In addition to copy number amplification, a beneficial single nucleotide variant arose in the K3L gene in some populations, resulting in a His47Arg amino acid change (K3LHis47Arg), which encodes enhanced inhibition of PKR activity and aids virus replication (Kawagishi-Kobayashi et al., 1997; Elde et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kawagishi-Kobayashi et al., 1997; Elde et al., 2012

claim: K3LHis47Arg encodes enhanced inhibition of PKR activity and aids virus replication.
source: In addition to copy number amplification, a beneficial single nucleotide variant arose in the K3L gene in some populations, resulting in a His47Arg amino acid change (K3LHis47Arg), which encodes enhanced inhibition of PKR activity and aids virus replication (Kawagishi-Kobayashi et al., 1997; Elde et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kawagishi-Kobayashi et al., 1997; Elde et al., 2012

claim: Virus titers remained well above parent (ΔE3L) levels through P20.
source: Comparative replication in human cells showed that virus titers remained well above parent (ΔE3L) levels through P20 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: A clear increase in replication around P5 coincided with the emergence of K3L CNV within virus genomes.
source: A clear increase in replication around P5 coincided with the emergence of K3L CNV within virus genomes (Elde et al., 2012), and gene copy number increases appeared to stabilize by P10 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Elde et al., 2012

claim: Gene copy number increases appeared to stabilize by P10.
source: A clear increase in replication around P5 coincided with the emergence of K3L CNV within virus genomes (Elde et al., 2012), and gene copy number increases appeared to stabilize by P10 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The K3LHis47Arg SNV was stable at an estimated frequency of 0.1 in the population from P5 through P10.
source: Notably, the K3LHis47Arg SNV, though apparently stable at an estimated frequency of 0.1 in the population from P5 through P10 (Elde et al., 2012), accumulated to near fixation between P10 and P20 (maximum frequency of approximately 0.9; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by citation to Elde et al., 2012 and data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The K3LHis47Arg SNV accumulated to near fixation between P10 and P20 with a maximum frequency of approximately 0.9.
source: Notably, the K3LHis47Arg SNV, though apparently stable at an estimated frequency of 0.1 in the population from P5 through P10 (Elde et al., 2012), accumulated to near fixation between P10 and P20 (maximum frequency of approximately 0.9; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The accumulation of the beneficial point mutation suggests that there is selection for the K3LHis47Arg variant in the heterogeneous virus population.
source: Thus, despite a plateau in replication across later experimental passages, the accumulation of the beneficial point mutation suggests that there is selection for the K3LHis47Arg variant in the heterogeneous virus population.
evidence: Inference based on experimental observations

claim: Either the K3LHis47Arg variant or K3L CNV is sufficient for a replication gain in human cells.
source: Comparing the ability of these viruses to replicate in human cells revealed that either the K3LHis47Arg variant or K3L CNV is sufficient for a replication gain, and the combination of the two genetic changes increases replication more than either one alone (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: The combination of K3LHis47Arg variant and K3L CNV increases replication more than either one alone in human cells.
source: Comparing the ability of these viruses to replicate in human cells revealed that either the K3LHis47Arg variant or K3L CNV is sufficient for a replication gain, and the combination of the two genetic changes increases replication more than either one alone (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: In a permissive hamster cell line, there was less than a 2-fold difference in titer between any of the four virus variants.
source: In contrast, in a permissive hamster cell line, there was less than a 2-fold difference in titer between any of these four viruses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: K3L containing the His47Arg variant is a more potent inhibitor of human PKR than wild-type K3L.
source: These results are consistent with earlier reports showing that K3L containing the His47Arg variant is a more potent inhibitor of human PKR than wild-type K3L (Kawagishi-Kobayashi et al., 1997), and that CNV was sufficient for overexpression of the K3L protein, which increased virus replication in human cells (Elde et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kawagishi-Kobayashi et al., 1997

claim: CNV was sufficient for overexpression of the K3L protein, which increased virus replication in human cells.
source: These results are consistent with earlier reports showing that K3L containing the His47Arg variant is a more potent inhibitor of human PKR than wild-type K3L (Kawagishi-Kobayashi et al., 1997), and that CNV was sufficient for overexpression of the K3L protein, which increased virus replication in human cells (Elde et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Elde et al., 2012

claim: Copy number affected K3LHis47Arg accumulation.
source: However, the K3LHis47Arg variant only reached high frequency in our experimental population following increases in K3L copy number. This suggests that copy number affected K3LHis47Arg accumulation, which could occur through changes to selection for the variant, recombination rate, replication rate, or some combination of these processes.
evidence: Inference based on experimental observations

claim: Apart from the K3LHis47Arg variant, only one other SNV was identified above an allele frequency of 0.01 in any of the sequenced populations compared to the parent ΔE3L virus.
source: Apart from the K3LHis47Arg variant, only one other SNV was identified above an allele frequency of 0.01 in any of the sequenced populations compared to the parent ΔE3L virus.
evidence: Supported by Illumina sequencing data analysis

claim: The E9LGlu495Gly variant is a point mutation encoding a Glu495Gly amino acid change in the viral DNA polymerase.
source: This variant, a point mutation encoding a Glu495Gly amino acid change in the viral DNA polymerase (E9LGlu495Gly), decreased in frequency from P10-P20, in contrast to the K3LHis47Arg SNV (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The E9LGlu495Gly variant decreased in frequency from P10-P20.
source: This variant, a point mutation encoding a Glu495Gly amino acid change in the viral DNA polymerase (E9LGlu495Gly), decreased in frequency from P10-P20, in contrast to the K3LHis47Arg SNV (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The E9LGlu495Gly SNV reached high frequency at P10 (0.64).
source: While the E9LGlu495Gly SNV reached high frequency at P10 (0.64), this variant alone did not provide a measurable increase in virus replication (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that it may be non-adaptive, and could have accumulated as a hitchhiker mutation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The E9LGlu495Gly variant alone did not provide a measurable increase in virus replication.
source: While the E9LGlu495Gly SNV reached high frequency at P10 (0.64), this variant alone did not provide a measurable increase in virus replication (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that it may be non-adaptive, and could have accumulated as a hitchhiker mutation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: The E9LGlu495Gly variant may be non-adaptive and could have accumulated as a hitchhiker mutation.
source: While the E9LGlu495Gly SNV reached high frequency at P10 (0.64), this variant alone did not provide a measurable increase in virus replication (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that it may be non-adaptive, and could have accumulated as a hitchhiker mutation.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data

claim: The detection of only two high-frequency SNVs reflects the rarity of point mutations during poxvirus replication relative to RNA viruses.
source: These observations, and the lack of any other detectable genetic changes, suggest that virus gains in replication were dominated by changes in K3L. Furthermore, the detection of only two high-frequency SNVs reflects the rarity of point mutations during poxvirus replication relative to RNA viruses and suggests that recombination-based mechanisms could be a major means of adaptation.
evidence: Inference based on experimental observations and established knowledge

claim: Recombination-based mechanisms could be a major means of adaptation in poxviruses.
source: These observations, and the lack of any other detectable genetic changes, suggest that virus gains in replication were dominated by changes in K3L. Furthermore, the detection of only two high-frequency SNVs reflects the rarity of point mutations during poxvirus replication relative to RNA viruses and suggests that recombination-based mechanisms could be a major means of adaptation.
evidence: Inference based on experimental observations

claim: Two distinct breakpoints flanking K3L were identified in the P10 population that differ by only 3 bp.
source: We previously identified two distinct breakpoints flanking K3L in the P10 population that differ by only 3 bp (Elde et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Elde et al., 2012

claim: Each of the two breakpoint pairs demarcates a duplicon approximately 500 bp in length.
source: Each of these breakpoint pairs demarcates a duplicon approximately 500 bp in length (Figure 2A), and encompasses both the K3L open reading frame (ORF, 267 bp) and predicted K3L promoter (Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Yang et al., 2010

claim: The duplicon encompasses both the K3L open reading frame (ORF, 267 bp) and predicted K3L promoter.
source: Each of these breakpoint pairs demarcates a duplicon approximately 500 bp in length (Figure 2A), and encompasses both the K3L open reading frame (ORF, 267 bp) and predicted K3L promoter (Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Yang et al., 2010

claim: Short Illumina reads cannot discriminate the presence or absence of the K3LHis47Arg variant either in single-copy K3L genomes or within multicopy arrays of K3L in heterogeneous virus populations.
source: In heterogeneous virus populations, short (e.g. 150 bp) Illumina reads cannot discriminate the presence or absence of the K3LHis47Arg variant either in single-copy K3L genomes or within multicopy arrays of K3L (Figure 2A).
evidence: Logical inference based on read length limitations

claim: ONT MinION sequencing routinely generated reads with a mean length of ~3 kbp and a N50 between 5–8 kbp.
source: Therefore, we sequenced virus genomes using the ONT MinION sequencing platform and routinely generated reads with a mean length of ~3 kbp and a N50 between 5–8 kbp (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Table 1

claim: ONT reads reached a maximum aligned length of 40 kbp with a standard library preparation.
source: These reads reached a maximum aligned length of 40 kbp with a standard library preparation (see Materials and methods for further details) and allowed us to directly measure both K3L copy number and the presence or absence of K3LHis47Arg in each K3L copy within individual virus genomes (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: ONT reads allowed direct measurement of both K3L copy number and the presence or absence of K3LHis47Arg in each K3L copy within individual virus genomes.
source: These reads reached a maximum aligned length of 40 kbp with a standard library preparation (see Materials and methods for further details) and allowed us to directly measure both K3L copy number and the presence or absence of K3LHis47Arg in each K3L copy within individual virus genomes (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: ONT reads yielded similar population-level allele frequencies to those estimated using Illumina MiSeq data for the same samples.
source: Using ONT reads, we performed variant calling on the two high frequency SNVs (K3LHis47Arg and E9LGlu495Gly) from every fifth passage, yielding similar population-level allele frequencies to those estimated using Illumina MiSeq data for the same samples (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Elde et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: ONT sequencing error rates are higher than in Illumina sequencing.
source: ONT sequencing error rates, which vary according to the specific k-mer being sequenced (Jain et al., 2018), are higher than in Illumina sequencing.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jain et al., 2018 and established knowledge

claim: The highest ONT error rate was only 2.6%.
source: While error rates differ between ONT flow cell chemistries, we found that the highest error rate was only 2.6% (Table 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), supporting the utility of ONT reads for identifying high frequency SNVs in virus genomes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Table 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The same two K3L duplication breakpoints previously described in the P10 population were identified using nanopore reads from P5, P10, P15, and P20.
source: We also identified the same two K3L duplication breakpoints previously described in the P10 population (Elde et al., 2012) using nanopore reads from P5, P10, P15, and P20, which revealed that the ~500 bp duplicons were maintained in the virus population throughout passaging (Table 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Table 3 and citation to Elde et al., 2012

claim: The ~500 bp duplicons were maintained in the virus population throughout passaging.
source: We also identified the same two K3L duplication breakpoints previously described in the P10 population (Elde et al., 2012) using nanopore reads from P5, P10, P15, and P20, which revealed that the ~500 bp duplicons were maintained in the virus population throughout passaging (Table 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Table 3

claim: K3L copy number expansions occurred as early as P5.
source: The long read datasets revealed that K3L copy number expansions occurred as early as P5 (Figure 2C), consistent with Southern blot analysis (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 1B

claim: Nearly 70% of virus genomes contained multiple copies of K3L by P10.
source: Over the course of the next five passages, K3L copy number steadily increased, and nearly 70% of virus genomes contained multiple copies of the gene by P10 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: From passages 10 to 20, there was a modest shift toward higher copy number arrays.
source: From passages 10 to 20, there was a modest shift toward higher copy number arrays, but the distribution of K3L copy number within the population appears to have reached a point near equilibrium.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Over 90% of sequenced virus genomes contained between 1 and 5 copies of K3L throughout the experiment.
source: Throughout the experiment, over 90% of sequenced virus genomes contained between 1 and 5 copies of K3L (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: The results are consistent with a fitness trade-off between additional K3L duplications and increased genome size at very high copy numbers.
source: These results, combined with the rapid collapse of copy number under relaxed selection (Figure 1C, Elde et al., 2012), are consistent with a fitness trade-off between additional K3L duplications and increased genome size at very high copy numbers.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data and citation to Elde et al., 2012

claim: Reads from genomes containing up to 16 total copies of K3L were captured using ONT.
source: However, using ONT, we captured reads from genomes containing up to 16 total copies of K3L (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), confirming that rare, large gene arrays exist in the population.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: The specific long read library preparation produced a mean read length of 9,392 bp (N50 = 19,288 bp), with a maximum aligned read length of 99,214 bp.
source: The alternate protocol produced a mean read length of 9,392 bp (N50 = 19,288 bp), with a maximum aligned read length of 99,214 bp (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Nearly 100 reads span a ~ 30 kbp region separating the two high frequency single nucleotide variants K3LHis47Arg and E9LGlu495Gly.
source: Using this specific long read preparation, we were also able to identify nearly 100 reads that span a ~ 30 kbp region separating the two high frequency single nucleotide variants in this population, K3LHis47Arg and E9LGlu495Gly (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Extremely long sequencing reads enable the direct phasing of distant variants within single poxvirus genomes.
source: These extremely long sequencing reads enable the direct phasing of distant variants within single poxvirus genomes, and suggest that single reads may routinely capture entire poxvirus genomes in future studies.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data

claim: Single reads may routinely capture entire poxvirus genomes in future studies.
source: These extremely long sequencing reads enable the direct phasing of distant variants within single poxvirus genomes, and suggest that single reads may routinely capture entire poxvirus genomes in future studies.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental data

claim: At P5, the K3LHis47Arg SNV was observed almost exclusively in single-copy reads.
source: At P5, the K3LHis47Arg SNV was observed almost exclusively in single-copy reads (four multicopy reads contained the SNV, compared to 304 single-copy reads; Figure 3), indicating that the variant likely originated in a single-copy genome.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: The K3LHis47Arg variant likely originated in a single-copy genome.
source: At P5, the K3LHis47Arg SNV was observed almost exclusively in single-copy reads (four multicopy reads contained the SNV, compared to 304 single-copy reads; Figure 3), indicating that the variant likely originated in a single-copy genome.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data

claim: From P5 to P10, there was a slight increase in the proportion of multicopy genomes containing the K3LHis47Arg SNV, which was enriched for mixed, rather than homogeneous K3LHis47Arg arrays.
source: From P5 to P10, while the K3LHis47Arg variant remained at a nearly constant population-level frequency (Figure 2B), we observed a slight increase in the proportion of multicopy genomes containing the SNV, which was enriched for mixed, rather than homogeneous K3LHis47Arg arrays (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: The scarcity of homogeneous K3LHis47Arg arrays at P10 suggests that the SNV entered multicopy arrays through recombination, rather than gene amplification from single copies of K3LHis47Arg.
source: Thus, even though the K3LHis47Arg SNV was present in a high proportion of single-copy reads by P5, the scarcity of homogeneous K3LHis47Arg arrays at P10 suggests that the SNV entered multicopy arrays through recombination, rather than gene amplification from single copies of K3LHis47Arg.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data

claim: From passages 10–20, homogeneous K3LHis47Arg arrays became increasingly prevalent, and were observed more frequently than mixed arrays.
source: From passages 10–20, as the K3LHis47Arg allele frequency drastically increased in the population (Figure 2B), we observed a very different pattern in the K3L arrays. By the last passages of the experiments, homogeneous K3LHis47Arg arrays became increasingly prevalent, and were observed more frequently than mixed arrays (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: Simulated K3LHis47Arg accumulation in passages 10–20 according to a binomial distribution showed a markedly lower prevalence of homogeneous K3L multicopy arrays compared to experimental data.
source: In contrast, when we simulated K3LHis47Arg accumulation in passages 10–20 according to a binomial distribution, we observed a markedly lower prevalence of homogeneous K3L multicopy arrays (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, see Materials and methods for further details).
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Despite having distinct error rate profiles, each ONT flowcell chemistry yielded nearly identical distributions of homogeneous and mixed K3L arrays.
source: First, we sequenced the P15 population with a variety of flowcell chemistries. Despite having distinct error rate profiles, each chemistry yielded nearly identical distributions of homogeneous and mixed K3L arrays (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: The experimental data consistently returned substantially higher fractions of mixed arrays compared to simulations, confirming that the observed enrichment of mixed arrays was not an artifact of sequencing errors.
source: From this analysis, the experimental data consistently returned substantially higher fractions of mixed arrays compared to the 1000 simulations, confirming that our observed enrichment of mixed arrays was not an artifact of sequencing errors (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: Every possible combination of K3LWT and K3LHis47Arg alleles was observed in K3L arrays with 3 or 4 copies of the gene at P15.
source: In K3L arrays with 3 or 4 copies of the gene, we observed every possible combination of K3LWT and K3LHis47Arg alleles at P15 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–B

claim: Mixed arrays remained prevalent in these populations, comprising between 23–42% of all 3-copy K3L arrays.
source: Mixed arrays remained prevalent in these populations, comprising between 23–42% of all 3-copy K3L arrays (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4A

claim: The abundance of mixed arrays, coupled with observation of numerous allele combinations and the low point mutation rate of poxviruses, strongly support a recombination-based mechanism of variant homogenization.
source: The abundance of mixed arrays, coupled with our observation of numerous allele combinations and the low point mutation rate of poxviruses (Gago et al., 2009; Sanjuán et al., 2010), strongly support a recombination-based mechanism of variant homogenization.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data and citations to Gago et al., 2009; Sanjuán et al., 2010

claim: Negligible sequencing error rates demonstrate that mixed arrays are not technical artifacts.
source: Consistent with this idea, negligible sequencing error rates observed in our identification of K3L alleles demonstrate that mixed arrays are not technical artifacts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and that replacement of K3LWT arrays with pure K3LHis47Arg arrays is not the primary means of variant homogenization (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: Replacement of K3LWT arrays with pure K3LHis47Arg arrays is not the primary means of variant homogenization.
source: Consistent with this idea, negligible sequencing error rates observed in our identification of K3L alleles demonstrate that mixed arrays are not technical artifacts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and that replacement of K3LWT arrays with pure K3LHis47Arg arrays is not the primary means of variant homogenization (Figure 3).
evidence: Inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: The K3LHis47Arg SNV was nearly equally distributed throughout K3L arrays, regardless of K3L copy number.
source: Throughout the passaging experiment, the K3LHis47Arg SNV was nearly equally distributed throughout K3L arrays, regardless of K3L copy number (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The same striking pattern of homogeneity for the K3LHis47Arg SNV was observed regardless of array copy number or a copy's position within the array, even when homogeneous K3LWT or K3LHis47Arg genomes were excluded.
source: To determine whether the presence of homogeneous K3L arrays, either K3LWT or K3LHis47Arg, influenced this pattern, we reanalyzed P15 virus genomes after removing all homogeneous K3L arrays from the dataset (Figure 4B). We observed the same striking pattern of homogeneity for the SNV, regardless of array copy number or a copy's position within the array.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Once the K3LHis47Arg variant entered multicopy genomes, variant accumulation was independent of copy number.
source: Because the same K3LHis47Arg SNV frequency is observed even when homogeneous K3LWT or K3LHis47Arg genomes are excluded, these results suggest that once the K3LHis47Arg variant entered multicopy genomes, variant accumulation was independent of copy number.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data

claim: All four P15 populations returned similar distributions of K3L copy number, as well as distributions of homogeneous and mixed arrays, regardless of MOI.
source: Analysis of all four P15 populations returned similar distributions of K3L copy number, as well as distributions of homogeneous and mixed arrays, regardless of MOI (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: Patterns of variant accumulation are robust to changes in the probability of intergenomic recombination.
source: Thus, even when co-infection is rare at the lowest MOI, these distributions are consistent, suggesting that patterns of variant accumulation are robust to changes in the probability of intergenomic recombination.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data

claim: Intragenomic recombination during replication from single virus infections is likely the main source for rapid homogenization of the K3LHis47Arg variant within gene arrays.
source: Therefore, intragenomic recombination during replication from single virus infections is likely the main source for rapid homogenization of the K3LHis47Arg variant within gene arrays.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data

claim: The initial presence of multicopy arrays containing mixed alleles, quickly followed by the predominance of multicopy arrays homogeneous for the variant is consistent with abundant intragenomic recombination resulting in a process reminiscent of gene conversion.
source: However, the initial presence of multicopy arrays containing mixed alleles, quickly followed by the predominance of multicopy arrays homogeneous for the variant (Figure 3) is also consistent with abundant intragenomic recombination resulting in a process reminiscent of gene conversion.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: A uniform reduction of K3L copy number was observed in the population following five passages in BHK cells (P15-BHK).
source: Consistent with related protocols of plaque purification in BHK cells (Figure 1C), we observed a uniform reduction of K3L copy number in the population following five passages in BHK cells (P15-BHK; Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A

claim: The K3LHis47Arg variant had not increased in frequency compared to P10 following passaging in BHK cells, in contrast to its accumulation in HeLa cells.
source: Further analysis of virus genomes from the P15-BHK population revealed that the K3LHis47Arg variant had not increased in frequency compared to P10, in contrast to its accumulation in HeLa cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The proportion of reads homogeneous for K3LHis47Arg decreased following passaging in BHK cells, as opposed to the rapid homogenization observed in HeLa cells.
source: Additionally, the proportion of reads homogeneous for K3LHis47Arg decreased following passaging in BHK cells (Figure 6C), as opposed to the rapid homogenization observed in HeLa cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Variant accumulation and homogenization are dependent on selective pressure imposed by the host environment.
source: These results suggest that variant accumulation and homogenization are dependent on selective pressure imposed by the host environment.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data

claim: Only the K3LHis47Arg variant reached near-fixation following passaging in human cells, while the E9LGlu495Gly variant decreased over the course of passaging in both HeLa and BHK cells.
source: Indeed, only the K3LHis47Arg variant reached near-fixation following passaging in human cells, while the E9LGlu495Gly variant instead decreased over the course of passaging in both HeLa and BHK cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6B

claim: One K3L breakpoint was dominant over the other, and the frequency of these breakpoints did not appreciably change over the course of passaging in either cell line.
source: Across all analyzed populations, we observed that one breakpoint was dominant over the other, and that the frequency of these breakpoints did not appreciably change over the course of passaging in either cell line (Table 3 and Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Table 3 and Figure 6D

claim: The consistency of neutral genetic changes sharply contrasts the rapid accumulation of the K3LHis47Arg variant in response to selection.
source: The consistency of these neutral genetic changes sharply contrasts the rapid accumulation of the K3LHis47Arg variant in response to selection, providing further support for the idea that selection is required to drive rapid homogenization of the K3LHis47Arg allele.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data

claim: The frequencies of the K3LHis47Arg SNV and the K3L breakpoints are uncoupled, despite their proximity in the genome.
source: Additionally, we observed that the frequencies of the K3LHis47Arg SNV and the K3L breakpoints are uncoupled (Figure 6B, Figure 6D), despite their proximity in the genome (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, Figure 6D, and Figure 2A

claim: The uncoupling of K3LHis47Arg SNV and K3L breakpoint frequencies supports gene conversion as a potentially major mechanism driving only the SNV to high frequency, rather than reciprocal recombination linking a particular breakpoint to the point mutation.
source: This observation supports gene conversion as a potentially major mechanism driving only the SNV to high frequency, rather than reciprocal recombination linking a particular breakpoint to the point mutation as it accumulated within the population.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data

claim: The results support a model of adaptation resembling gene conversion, in which a beneficial variant that enters an amplified gene array can be rapidly spread among the remaining copies through recombination and selection.
source: Taken together, our results support a model of adaptation resembling gene conversion, in which a beneficial variant that enters an amplified gene array can be rapidly spread among the remaining copies through recombination and selection (Figure 7).
evidence: Inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 7

claim: Repeated gene amplification likely also contributes to the accumulation of the beneficial SNV.
source: Repeated gene amplification likely also contributes to the accumulation of the beneficial SNV; however, the large proportions and various patterns of mixed allele combinations in multicopy arrays suggest that this is not the only mechanism of genome diversification.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data

claim: The consistency of neutral variants in close proximity to the rapidly homogenized SNV strongly support a model of recombination-driven homogenization.
source: Furthermore, while we cannot directly distinguish between gene conversion and crossover events, the consistency of neutral variants in close proximity to the rapidly homogenized SNV strongly support a model of recombination-driven homogenization.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data

claim: Gene conversion could be a unique adaptive feature of large DNA viruses.
source: This process could be a unique adaptive feature of large DNA viruses, because evolution through mechanisms of gene duplication are widespread in DNA viruses (McLysaght et al., 2003; Shackelton and Holmes, 2004; Filée, 2009; Elde et al., 2012; Filée, 2015; Gao et al., 2017), but rare in RNA viruses (Simon-Loriere and Holmes, 2013).
evidence: Speculation supported by citations

claim: Evolution through mechanisms of gene duplication are widespread in DNA viruses.
source: This process could be a unique adaptive feature of large DNA viruses, because evolution through mechanisms of gene duplication are widespread in DNA viruses (McLysaght et al., 2003; Shackelton and Holmes, 2004; Filée, 2009; Elde et al., 2012; Filée, 2015; Gao et al., 2017), but rare in RNA viruses (Simon-Loriere and Holmes, 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Gene duplication is rare in RNA viruses.
source: This process could be a unique adaptive feature of large DNA viruses, because evolution through mechanisms of gene duplication are widespread in DNA viruses (McLysaght et al., 2003; Shackelton and Holmes, 2004; Filée, 2009; Elde et al., 2012; Filée, 2015; Gao et al., 2017), but rare in RNA viruses (Simon-Loriere and Holmes, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Simon-Loriere and Holmes, 2013

claim: DNA viruses possess significantly lower point mutation rates than RNA viruses.
source: For DNA viruses, which possess significantly lower point mutation rates than RNA viruses (Gago et al., 2009; Sanjuán et al., 2010), the rapid fixation of rare beneficial variants within multiple gene copies could be key to the process of adaptation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Gago et al., 2009; Sanjuán et al., 2010

claim: The rapid fixation of rare beneficial variants within multiple gene copies could be key to the process of adaptation in DNA viruses.
source: For DNA viruses, which possess significantly lower point mutation rates than RNA viruses (Gago et al., 2009; Sanjuán et al., 2010), the rapid fixation of rare beneficial variants within multiple gene copies could be key to the process of adaptation.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental data and citations

claim: The rapid spread of point mutations in gene arrays would counter the advantages of single or low-copy genomes enriched for the SNV to dominate DNA virus populations.
source: A major outcome from genetic homogenization of beneficial point mutations in multicopy genes might be an enhanced persistence of large gene families. Under this model, the rapid spread of point mutations in gene arrays would counter the advantages of single or low-copy genomes enriched for the SNV to dominate DNA virus populations.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental findings

claim: Nearly half of the Canarypox genome consists of 14 gene families, which may have been regularly shaped by mechanisms of genetic homogenization.
source: Among poxviruses, for example, nearly half of the Canarypox genome consists of 14 gene families, which may have been regularly shaped by mechanisms of genetic homogenization (Afonso et al., 2000; Tulman et al., 2004).
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to Afonso et al., 2000; Tulman et al., 2004

claim: The Bodo saltan virus has a large gene family of 148 ankyrin repeat proteins at the ends of its linear genome, with some copies being nearly identical.
source: Within the emerging classes of giant viruses, the Bodo saltan virus is notable for a large gene family of 148 ankyrin repeat proteins at the ends of its linear genome, with some copies being nearly identical (Deeg et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Deeg et al., 2018

claim: Repeated homogenization through gene conversion has been suggested as the process driving concerted evolution of viral genes.
source: Indeed, repeated homogenization through gene conversion has been suggested as the process driving concerted evolution of viral genes (Hughes, 2004), which has been observed in nanoviruses (Hughes, 2004; Hu et al., 2007; Savory and Ramakrishnan, 2014), baculoviruses (de Andrade Zanotto and Krakauer, 2008), and Epstein-Barr virus, a human herpesvirus (Ba Abdullah et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Concerted evolution has been observed in nanoviruses.
source: Indeed, repeated homogenization through gene conversion has been suggested as the process driving concerted evolution of viral genes (Hughes, 2004), which has been observed in nanoviruses (Hughes, 2004; Hu et al., 2007; Savory and Ramakrishnan, 2014), baculoviruses (de Andrade Zanotto and Krakauer, 2008), and Epstein-Barr virus, a human herpesvirus (Ba Abdullah et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hughes, 2004; Hu et al., 2007; Savory and Ramakrishnan, 2014

claim: Concerted evolution has been observed in baculoviruses.
source: Indeed, repeated homogenization through gene conversion has been suggested as the process driving concerted evolution of viral genes (Hughes, 2004), which has been observed in nanoviruses (Hughes, 2004; Hu et al., 2007; Savory and Ramakrishnan, 2014), baculoviruses (de Andrade Zanotto and Krakauer, 2008), and Epstein-Barr virus, a human herpesvirus (Ba Abdullah et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to de Andrade Zanotto and Krakauer, 2008

claim: Concerted evolution has been observed in Epstein-Barr virus, a human herpesvirus.
source: Indeed, repeated homogenization through gene conversion has been suggested as the process driving concerted evolution of viral genes (Hughes, 2004), which has been observed in nanoviruses (Hughes, 2004; Hu et al., 2007; Savory and Ramakrishnan, 2014), baculoviruses (de Andrade Zanotto and Krakauer, 2008), and Epstein-Barr virus, a human herpesvirus (Ba Abdullah et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ba Abdullah et al., 2017

claim: Long read sequencing demonstrates the power to perform high resolution analyses of complex genome dynamics.
source: Our work also demonstrates the power of long read sequencing to perform high resolution analyses of complex genome dynamics.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data

claim: Using the Oxford Nanopore Technologies platform, two simultaneous adaptations were investigated at single-genome resolution.
source: Using the Oxford Nanopore Technologies platform, we investigated two simultaneous adaptations at single-genome resolution.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Long read sequencing provides a framework to definitively determine the sequence content of tandem gene duplications, and accurately call variants within these repetitive regions.
source: This type of analysis provides a framework to definitively determine the sequence content of tandem gene duplications, and accurately call variants within these repetitive regions.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data

claim: The longest reads obtained suggest that entire poxvirus genomes could routinely be captured in single reads.
source: Additionally, we demonstrate the ability to phase extremely distant genetic variants, and the longest reads we obtained suggest that entire poxvirus genomes could routinely be captured in single reads.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental data

claim: Sequencing entire DNA virus genomes with long reads could expand our understanding of DNA virus adaptation as a population evolves.
source: Sequencing entire DNA virus genomes with this level of detail could expand our understanding of DNA virus adaptation as a population evolves, either in an experimental system or during infection of a host.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental findings

claim: Long read sequencing methods allow for high-resolution analyses of complex genomes and could be used to explore the evolution of diverse organisms.
source: Together, these methods allow for high-resolution analyses of complex genomes and could be used to explore the evolution of diverse organisms in new and exciting detail.
evidence: Inference based on experimental findings
